title: Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the Legislature as SB 417 (Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026). Final legislative votes: Senate 29 ayes, 2 noes; Assembly 61 ayes, 7 noes.

question.text: AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including for California veterans, and to finance housing development projects seeking federal tax credits. Allocates funds: $5.1 billion to build and rehabilitate multifamily rental housing; $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate, or preserve affordable housing units, and provide supportive housing for those experiencing homelessness; $1.25 billion for state-funded mortgages for California veterans; $1.1 billion for homeownership and downpayment assistance; $1 billion for farmworker, tribal, and student housing; $500 million for housing infrastructure; and $200 million to support local housing programs.

summary.text: Allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds: a $10 billion bond for state housing programs repaid from the General Fund and a $1.25 billion bond for veterans home loans repaid by veterans' loan payments. Per the Legislative Analyst, funds go to affordable multifamily housing ($7.2 billion), homeownership programs ($1.1 billion), infrastructure ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing ($350 million), tribal housing ($200 million) and local pilot programs ($200 million). Fiscal impact: increased state General Fund cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years; the veterans program has operated at no direct state cost.

measure.yesMeans: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
measure.noMeans: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.

argumentsFor.text: Official argument in favor, signed by Anni Chung (Self-Help for the Elderly), Jeffery Freitas (California Federation of Teachers) and John H. Ing (US Vets): "Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting." It also says: "Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford."
Also in the official argument: "Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans' housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program."

argumentsAgainst.text: Sen. Tony Strickland (R-Huntington Beach), as quoted by CalMatters from a June legislative hearing: "It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond." CalMatters also reports he said there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to "borrow money against the future." (News report, not an official ballot argument; the official guide has no argument against.)

currentLaw.text: In most years about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California; for state-funded housing the state generally gives local governments, nonprofits and developers grants or low-cost loans, and the housing typically must go to low-income Californians. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing (2024) provided $2 billion for people facing homelessness with mental health or substance use challenges; the last veterans home loan bond (2018) provided $1 billion.

fiscalImpact.text: Legislative Analyst: repaying the $10 billion General Fund bond would cost $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years, about 0.25 percent of the General Fund budget, and total cost about 15 percent more (inflation-adjusted) than paying up front. Veterans' loan payments have always covered the $1.25 billion veterans bonds, so no direct state cost. Funds would subsidize up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, about 2,500 farmworker units and about 1,200 student beds, and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership.

supporters.text: Yes on Prop 1 committees registered with the Secretary of State: Yes on Prop 1 Californians for Homes, Jobs and Affordability 2026 (sponsored by affordable housing organizations); Californians for Affordable Homes, Yes on Proposition 1 (sponsored by NPH Action Fund); Yes on Prop 1, California Homeless and Housing Coalition Action Fund.
Self-Help for the Elderly, California Federation of Teachers and US Vets (signers of the official argument in favor).

Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium and California Alliance of Child and Family Services (named as supporters in the official argument in favor).
Gov. Gavin Newsom, California Democratic Party, AFL-CIO California and the California Apartment Association (listed as supporters in CalMatters' voter guide).

opponents.text: Sen. Tony Strickland (R-Huntington Beach), who opposed the bill in the Legislature; CalMatters reports two Republican senators and seven Republican assemblymembers voted no.
"Some Republican state lawmakers" (listed as opponents in CalMatters' voter guide).

campaignFinance.text: Support: $12,789,950 reported by three committees (Yes on Prop 1 Californians for Homes, Jobs and Affordability 2026, $11,383,978; Californians for Affordable Homes, $1,085,546; California Homeless and Housing Coalition Action Fund, $320,426). Opposition: no committees identified. Source: Cal-Access totals as compiled by the Secretary of State from specified reports, through 10/06/2026.
